entities.name: Great Mosque of Kairouan
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Great Mosque of Kairouan in Tunisia (Uqba Mosque), founded in 670 CE by Uqba ibn Nafi, the Arab general who established the city of Kairouan, is one of the oldest surviving mosques in the world, the most sacred religious site in North Africa, and the mosque from which all North African and Andalusian Islamic architecture derives. Kairouan — the first Islamic city in the Maghreb — was for centuries considered the fourth holiest city in Islam (after Mecca, Medina, and Jerusalem), and seven pilgrimages to Kairouan were considered equivalent to the Hajj.

The original 670 CE mosque was a simple courtyard structure; it was rebuilt by Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik (724 CE), then comprehensively reconstructed by the Aghlabid emirs (9th century) in its current form. The three-tiered minaret (the world's oldest surviving minaret, 9th century) became the model for minarets throughout North Africa, Spain, and Morocco. The horseshoe arches (using marble columns recycled from Roman Carthage), carved wooden minbar (oldest surviving in the Muslim world, 9th century), and mosaic mihrab (using Byzantine tiles) represent the architectural synthesis that defined Western Islamic aesthetics.

Kairouan's influence on Islamic scholarship was equal to its architectural importance: the Great Mosque's madrasa trained scholars who spread across the Maghreb. The Maliki school of Islamic law — the dominant school in North Africa and West Africa — was transmitted through Kairouan. The mosque's 9th-century wooden minbar, believed to have been commissioned around 862 CE and carved in Baghdad, is the oldest surviving minbar in the world — a 1,160-year-old wooden object that still functions.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Great Mosque of Kairouan — with the world's oldest surviving minaret, the oldest surviving wooden minbar, and the architectural source of all North African and Andalusian mosque design — is the most historically consequential mosque in the western Islamic world, whose forms and scholarship shaped 500 million Muslims' religious practice.
